Primase. A specialized RNA polymerase that synthesizes short RNA primers during DNA replication, providing the three-prime hydroxyl group that DNA polymerase requires to begin synthesis. Essential to the replication process, primase catalyzes the formation of primers on both the leading and lagging strands.

Primase belongs to the primase enzyme family, distinct from standard DNA polymerases. It synthesizes RNA rather than DNA, producing primers roughly eight to twelve nucleotides in length in prokaryotes. DNA polymerase cannot initiate synthesis from scratch. It requires a three-prime hydroxyl group already present to extend from, making primase essential for every replication event. Primase creates short RNA-DNA hybrid molecules—the primer plus the start of DNA synthesis. These primers are later removed and replaced with DNA by DNA polymerase one or other exonucleases and polymerases in eukaryotes. Primase acts continuously on the lagging strand to synthesize many primers for each Okazaki fragment, which comprises about a thousand nucleotides in prokaryotes or one hundred to two hundred in eukaryotes. But it only acts once on the leading strand. Primase couples with DNA polymerase three in prokaryotes or DNA polymerase alpha in eukaryotes. The polymerase immediately extends the primer synthesized by primase. In prokaryotes, primase functions as part of the primosome complex, a multiprotein assembly that couples primer synthesis with strand unwinding and polymerase loading. Primase is highly conserved across all domains of life—bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes—indicating its ancient and essential role in DNA metabolism.
